pr_body:
This pull request partially supersedes #30329, in that I've separated out the PKCE changes from the other changes.

As per [OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practices](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-27.html#name-authorization-code-grant), we MUST support PKCE.

Whilst PKCE is recommended for all applications to use, forcing PKCE usage is a breaking change, so for now we do not force PKCE usage, only support it. PKCE is an important security mechanism for preventing [OAuth Authorization Code Injection Attacks](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-27.html#name-pkce). **Note:** OAuth 2.1 requires the usage of PKCE.

In accordance with best practices, we only support S256, and explicitly do not support plain for PKCE `code_challenge_method`. Unfortunately, Doorkeeper [does not support](https://github.com/doorkeeper-gem/doorkeeper/issues/1717) a setting for which `code_challenge_method`s are supported, hence adding a `OauthPreAuthorizationExtension` module and changing the `doorkeeper.errors.messages.invalid_code_challenge_method` value.

I've also attempted to add some better tests to ensure certain elements are definitely present on the page, such that we're not just relying on the `response.body` containing a given string, but actually that the element exists.

Fixes: #21913
pr_comments:
First, to make sure I understand exactly the context, as I'm not so familiar with Doorkeepr and OAuth:
- PKCE is an extension of OAuth made so that the OAuth provider can ensure that the application that received the code is truly the one that requested it, before giving it the authentication token
- this is primarily meant for public clients, which Mastodon doesn't really support at the moment (which is a whole other issue), but can still be useful for confidential clients in some cases, and has no real drawback, and therefore is a MUST in the latest OAuth 2.0 best practices
- Doorkeeper does support it natively, provided the database has the correct columns and the parameters are passed properly
- there is some discussion regarding PKCE and refresh tokens (which we don't currently support either) but my understanding is that for the most part, those are orthogonal and refresh tokens do not typically involve a potentially unsecure channel, unlike the initial authentication

Please correct me if I'm wrong on any on this.

(Now I'll look at the code itself and especially where you tagged me)

@ClearlyClaire 
> this is primarily meant for public clients, which Mastodon doesn't really support at the moment (which is a whole other issue), but can still be useful for confidential clients in some cases, and has no real drawback, and therefore is a MUST in the latest OAuth 2.0 best practices

It was originally for public clients, but is now a MUST for all clients due to authorization code injection attacks.

> there is some discussion regarding PKCE and refresh tokens (which we don't currently support either) but my understanding is that for the most part, those are orthogonal and refresh tokens do not typically involve a potentially unsecure channel, unlike the initial authentication

tl;dr; let's disregard refresh tokens for now, and focus on PKCE. (#27948 has been made a draft to indicate it should **not** be in 4.3)

Doorkeeper's refresh token model is fundamentally broken though, because it doesn't keep trust chains (basically if you revoke the access token the refresh token can remain valid, and if you do a `access token -> refresh token -> access token -> refresh token` then there's something where the revocation of the original access token doesn't result in the second token set being revoked or something. (I'm still trying to get my head fully around this.

From Auth0:
- Refresh token rotation guarantees that every time an application exchanges a refresh token to get a new access token, a new refresh token is also returned.
- [Automatic Reuse Detection for Refresh Tokens](https://auth0.com/blog/refresh-tokens-what-are-they-and-when-to-use-them/#Refresh-Token-Automatic-Reuse-Detection)

tl;dr; is that you should actually have a separate oauth_refresh_tokens table, instead of just a column in the oauth_access_tokens table, as you need to be able to follow the chain of tokens.

> this is primarily meant for public clients, which Mastodon doesn't really support at the moment (which is a whole other issue),

Yeah, this is something I want to bring support for, but it's "complicated" — I need to fully review the implications of this, but work is started in #30329
Added an issue about Client ID Metadata Documents here: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/31151

issue_context.title: Support OAuth PKCE to allow third-party single-page apps to utilize best practice when authorizing with an instance
issue_context.body:
### Pitch

Mastodon [hasn't configured PKCE on Doorkeepr](https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/discussions/17207?sort=top#discussioncomment-1913479). Will it be possible to make that OAuth extension accessible?

Also, if PKCE is used, can the client secret _not_ be shared by the instance when the app registers with it?

### Motivation

If you are to write a third-party app that runs completely off the browser and it needs to authorize with an OAuth capable server, the best practice is to use ["the Authorization Code flow with the PKCE extension"](https://oauth.net/2/browser-based-apps/). Since Mastodon doesn't offer that extension, such a third-party client would have to store [the client secret in `localStorage`](https://github.com/takahashim/mastodon-access-token/blob/master/index.html#L189) in order to retrieve access tokens. Storing the client secrets in `localStorage` is [insecure](https://thesecurityvault.com/auth-token-in-localstorage/).

Why not create a backend to keep the client secret safe? Well now you have [to store the client secret for each mastodon instance in a database](https://github.com/diddledani/twitodon/blob/fd943cc163f516b4e943c529ae77f5a17f731407/api/mastodon.mjs#L39). Also, the creation of the backend is extra effort, complexity, and resources 💸.
comments:
Upon further review, PKCE was designed assuming apps could [only be registered once](https://developer.okta.com/blog/2019/05/01/is-the-oauth-implicit-flow-dead#the-oauth-authorization-code-flow-is-better). However, Mastodon instances allow you to register your client app multiple times as can be demonstrated with [the Access Token Generator](https://takahashim.github.io/mastodon-access-token/) I linked to above as an example of storing the client secret in `localStorage`.

Even with PKCE, you have to store the `code_verifier` in `localStorage` as seen in [this okta article's code example](https://developer.okta.com/blog/2019/05/01/is-the-oauth-implicit-flow-dead#begin-the-pkce-request). So really, the only difference I see between storing the `code_verifier` or the `client_secret` in `localStorage`, withinin the Mastodon auth code flow context, is the former is generated client-side and the later server-side. 

I'm gonna leave this request open in case others see a benefit in turning on PKCE on Mastodon (even OAuth recommends it to be used [in addition to client secrets](https://oauth.net/2/pkce/)). However, feel free to close it if the maintainers see no reason to support PKCE.

If I understand it correctly PKCE is currently not required for pure browser-based applications, because these have to register their own `client_id`+`client_secret` through the `POST /api/v1/apps`, which then kind of acts as a `code_verifier`. If you want to provide a "no trust required" tool, you can't have these on your server, though, because the server sees the oauth `code` in the GET Parameters and then could retrieve the access token without the user knowing. (Normally one would pre-register the application with a single instance and the `client_id` is public, so the `code_verifier` is required to restrict access to the access token to the browser, but here the `client_secret` is only known in the browser, so it should be fine?)

I think there still needs to be something done or clarified in regards to these pure browser based API consumers, though: The current setup requires these clients to register an application with the mastodon instance for every user of the app, possibly multiple times for each user (I think the linked Access Token Generator even does it every time you press the button). So that could add up to a lot of registered apps for a single application, which feels bad to me. Is that the intended workflow?

If yes Mastodon has to make sure, that either:
* There are regular cleanups running that purge registered apps from the database and having lots of them isn't a problem
  * I would not expect that to happen, though, because the normal workflow suggests only registering once and then storing and using that `client_id` and `client_secret` forever?
  * So maybe an additional flag is needed to mark a registered app as "temporary"?
* Or better: Registering the application with the mastodon instance is entirely stateless
  * For example: The Mastodon instance could "sign" the provided `scopes` + `redirect_uris`+ a salt + a secret with something like HMAC and return the result as a client-secret? (But unsure how to present/store stuff like `client_name` & `website` then? Could maybe also store these in `client_id`, so the client resends them when authorization happens)

Is something like this already happening, so it is fine to register multiple apps for each user of an application? Then this should be clarified in the documentation.
If this is not happening and we should refrain from creating applications that do that, that should also be clarified in the documentation and possibly fixed.
Yes, this would be great please.

As PKCE is now a OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, I'm going to try to get this into 4.3, such that in a future version we can enforce usage of PKCE for all clients: https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-27.html#name-authorization-code-grant

review_comments:
All those new examples here seem to test the user interface and as such do not belong in a "controller spec".

There are two alternative options:

* If you just want to make sure certain things are present in the html template, then a "view spec" would be the correct place. Additionally you _could_ add a test here that makes sure the controller actually renders that template.
* If you want to make sure that a certain kind of client request leads to the UI being in a certain state, this should be a "system spec". If you go down that route, you might want to have these be "driven_by" `:rack_test` which is a lot faster than spinning up a browser for this (see https://rspec.info/features/6-0/rspec-rails/system-specs/system-specs/)

I do agree, though as we were already doing the controller spec like this (assertions on response body) I'd like to run with this as-is, and create a follow up issue to address controller vs request vs system tests for OAuth flows

I feel like system specs are probably most relevant for OAuth flows, not controller or request or view specs

Maybe we'd have a controller spec that just asserts out custom views for doorkeeper get rendered?

(also, I try really hard to limit scope of changes due to frequently being asked to break PRs down into smaller chunks, which takes significant time)

Just to be super-clear: I am not suggesting creating generic oauth flow system specs. Just moving these here out to either a view or a (single) system spec file. This would not widen the scope of this PR, just make better use of the different kinds of spec types `rspec-rails` provides.

I'm going to wait for @ClearlyClaire's input here, since I don't want to risk overcomplicating this PR by rewriting a known working test too heavily (as it is I only made the changes I did because the assertions were quiet weak & could lead to tests passing when they shouldn't

I agree with @oneiros that this kind of tests belong in system tests. I'd suggest looking at the existing `spec/system/oauth_spec.rb` tests to see if those could be moved there instead without a lot more effort, but if that amount of work is prohibitive at the moment, I'm ok with the consolidation happening in another PR (note that I have not actually reviewed the specs yet, just quickly read through them, and I'm commenting on the general approach)

Yeah, I'd like to do a review of the oauth specs as a separate task after implement PKCE. Only reason I noticed was because they were already doing stuff like

```
        expect(response.body).to match(/Authorize/)
```

Which isn't great at all, because the string Authorize could appear *anywhere* on the response body.
Have created https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/31150 to track the OAuth Specs state.
For some reason #29191 didn't actually include tests for these, despite them being present.
I'm honestly not sure I've done this in the "correct" way, but it's temporary until https://github.com/doorkeeper-gem/doorkeeper/issues/1717 is resolved.
Given that, I believe it is totally fine for now.
